lead: Polymer properties are decided before the product is shaped: by how regular each chain is, how much it branches, whether chains are joined to each other, and how long they are. Regular unbranched chains pack closely and form crystalline regions. Irregular chains pack loosely and stay amorphous. Packing controls density, stiffness, softening point, transparency and flexibility. This is why a polyethylene bag, a water pipe and cable insulation can all be polyethylene yet behave differently.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for polymer terms and classification, 5.2 for tacticity, and 5.3 for branching routes.

sections.h3: Regular chains pack; irregular chains do not

blocks.text: A linear chain with small, regularly placed side groups can slide beside its neighbours. van der Waals forces and dipole forces then hold short stretches in ordered, parallel bundles. These ordered regions are crystallites; the rest is amorphous. Isotactic and syndiotactic chains can crystallise. Atactic chains cannot, because side groups stick out randomly and keep neighbours apart. See 5.2 for tacticity.

blocks.where: w<sub>c</sub> is mass fraction crystalline; ρ is sample density; ρ<sub>a</sub> is density of fully amorphous sample; ρ<sub>c</sub> is density of fully crystalline sample. All densities in g/cm³.

blocks.text: Crystallinity raises density because chains fit closer. It also raises stiffness and melting point, and lowers transparency because crystallites scatter light. A clear bag is mostly amorphous; a stiff milk jug is more crystalline. The same trade-off explains why high-density polyethylene is opaque and strong while low-density polyethylene is translucent and flexible.
Packing is not all-or-nothing. A polymer is semicrystalline: crystallites sit in an amorphous matrix. The fraction w<sub>c</sub> is measured from density. The worked example below uses this formula.

sections.h3: Branching, cross-linking, molar mass and forces

blocks.text: Branching blocks packing. Low-density polyethylene (LDPE) has many long and short branches, so chains cannot align well; it is soft, translucent and low melting. High-density polyethylene (HDPE) is almost linear; it packs well, is denser, stiffer and used for pipes and bottles. Branching routes are in 5.3.

Cross-linking ties chains into a network. A thermoset such as cured epoxy cannot be melted or dissolved because the network holds its shape. Vulcanised rubber has sulphur bridges between chains. Cross-linking raises stiffness and prevents flow, but too much cross-linking makes rubber hard and brittle.

Molar mass also matters. Longer chains entangle more, so strength and viscosity rise with average molar mass. Very short chains act like a lubricant and weaken the material. Molar mass averages are covered in 5.7.

Intermolecular forces add to packing. Nylon chains have amide groups that hydrogen-bond, so nylon is strong and has a high melting point even without covalent cross-links. PVC has polar C–Cl dipoles; dipole forces make it rigid at room temperature. Polyethylene has only weak dispersion forces, so it softens at lower temperature. Named polymers are in 5.6.

Two temperatures describe softening. The glass transition temperature T<sub>g</sub> is the temperature below which amorphous regions are glassy and rigid; above T<sub>g</sub> they become rubbery and can move. T<sub>g</sub> is not a sharp melting point; it is a range measured by a standard method.

The melting point T<sub>m</sub> is the temperature at which crystalline regions melt. A semicrystalline polymer has both T<sub>g</sub> and T<sub>m</sub>; an amorphous polymer has only T<sub>g</sub>. High crystallinity raises T<sub>m</sub> and stiffness. Plasticiser molecules sit between chains, lower T<sub>g</sub> and make PVC flexible for wires and upholstery.

Elastomers are a special case. Above T<sub>g</sub>, rubber chains are coiled and tangled. A pull straightens and uncoils them; on release, thermal motion recoils them. Sulphur cross-links stop chains from sliding past each other, so the rubber returns to shape instead of flowing. This is elastomer elasticity.
At room temperature, natural rubber and silicone rubber are rubbery; polystyrene and PMMA are glassy; LDPE is soft and waxy; HDPE is stiff.

figure.caption: A regular linear chain packs into crystalline regions and gives a stiff, high-melting solid; a branched or atactic chain packs poorly and gives a soft, low-melting solid. Notice that the two outcomes come from packing, not from a new chemical reaction.

spec.title: Two chains, two behaviours
spec.aria: Two parallel chains of cause and effect: a regular linear chain packs into a crystalline stiff solid, while a branched chain packs poorly and stays soft.

examples.question: A polyethylene sample has density ρ = 0.940 g/cm³. The fully amorphous density is ρa = 0.850 g/cm³ and the fully crystalline density is ρc = 1.000 g/cm³. Calculate the mass fraction of crystallinity and the percentage crystallinity.
steps: Use the two-phase density formula: wc = ρc(ρ − ρa) ÷ [ρ(ρc − ρa)].
examples.answer: The mass fraction crystalline is 0.638, that is 63.8% crystalline.
examples.check:
rho = 0.940
rho_a = 0.850
rho_c = 1.000
wc = rho_c * (rho - rho_a) / (rho * (rho_c - rho_a))
print(f"{wc:.3f}")
print(f"{wc*100:.1f}")

traps: Do not say higher crystallinity makes a polymer both stronger and clearer: it raises stiffness and density but lowers transparency because crystallites scatter light.
Do not confuse branching with cross-linking: branches prevent packing but do not join chains; cross-links join chains and stop flow.
T<sub>g</sub> applies to amorphous regions; T<sub>m</sub> applies to crystalline regions. An amorphous polymer has T<sub>g</sub> but no T<sub>m</sub>.
Do not use volume fraction in the density formula unless stated; the formula gives mass fraction w<sub>c</sub>. Keep all densities in the same units.
Atactic does not mean branched. Atactic means random side-group orientation; branching means side chains.

quiz.q: Define glass transition temperature and melting point for a polymer.
quiz.a: T<sub>g</sub> is the temperature below which amorphous regions are glassy and above which they become rubbery. T<sub>m</sub> is the temperature at which crystalline regions melt.

quiz.q: Why does HDPE have higher density and stiffness than LDPE?
quiz.a: HDPE is almost linear, so chains pack closely into crystalline regions. LDPE is branched, so chains cannot pack well and remain more amorphous. Closer packing gives higher density and stiffness.

quiz.q: A polymer sample has ρ = 0.920 g/cm³, ρ<sub>a</sub> = 0.850 g/cm³ and ρ<sub>c</sub> = 1.000 g/cm³. Find the mass fraction crystalline.
Why does vulcanisation make rubber stronger and prevent flow, while keeping it elastic?
quiz.a: Sulphur cross-links join chains into a network. The network stops chains from sliding past each other, so the rubber cannot flow. The chains can still uncoil and recoil between cross-links, so the rubber remains elastic.

quiz.q: Nylon has no covalent cross-links, yet it is strong and high melting. Explain.
quiz.a: Nylon chains have amide groups that form hydrogen bonds between neighbouring chains. These strong intermolecular forces hold chains together, raise stiffness and raise the melting point.

quiz.q: A polymer has T<sub>g</sub> = −60 °C. At room temperature, 25 °C, is its amorphous part glassy or rubbery?
quiz.a: Room temperature is above T<sub>g</sub>, so the amorphous part is rubbery, not glassy.

quiz.q: A transparent semicrystalline polymer becomes opaque after annealing. What structural change is most likely?
quiz.a: Annealing allows chains to pack better, so crystallinity increases. Larger crystallites scatter visible light, making the polymer opaque. Density and stiffness also rise, while flexibility falls.

beyond: Not for the exam. Polymer structure–property maps guide the choice of grades for packaging, pipes, tyres and medical devices. Industry uses differential scanning calorimetry to measure T<sub>g</sub> and T<sub>m</sub>, and gel permeation chromatography to measure molar mass. Search for “structure–property relationship of polymers”, “crystallinity density method”, and “vulcanisation”. Newer curricula add polymer recycling and biodegradable polyesters, where crystallinity controls both strength and compostability.
